Checked both. Here is where they stand.

## "Decisive at H≥192" is not defensible

`scripts/backbone_toggle_core.py` is the clean single-variable control: identical Residual-IA+ recipe, same seeds, same schedule, same shared NLinear raw branch, the only change being `backbone_off` zeroing the residual gate. It refutes the claim (positive = the backbone path makes MSE **worse**, n=3 per cell, MOMENT-small):

| dataset | H=96 | H=192 | H=336 | H=720 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ETTh1 | +1.81% | +6.34% | +5.16% | **+26.69%** |
| ETTh2 | +4.43% | −0.94% | +5.54% | +4.55% |
| ETTm1 | +0.22% | −1.16% | +1.87% | +2.38% |
| ETTm2 | +5.87% | +1.83% | +0.40% | +3.05% |
| Weather | −3.08% | −3.89% | −3.21% | −4.40% |
| Electricity | +2.69% | +2.04% | +3.16% | +2.86% |
| **mean** | +1.99% | **+0.70%** | +2.15% | +5.85% |
| helps | 1/6 | 3/6 | 1/6 | 1/6 |

At H=192, the horizon where round 1 said the backbone is decisive, it costs 0.70% on average and helps on three datasets by at most 3.89%. The trend runs the wrong way with horizon, not the right way.

## The 18/18 is real; only its description was wrong

`results/tsfm_earns_keep` reproduces exactly: 18/18 cells, per-cell mean **−11.79%**, matching round 1's "−11.8%". But the comparison arm is the backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE, which swaps two variables at once, no backbone **and** an MLP raw branch instead of NLinear. The script's own docstring says so. So the number stands and the attribution does not. That is your fallback if pressed: the result is genuine, it just cannot isolate the backbone.

## "Not dead weight" survives only in the scoped form

Weather is the one dataset where the frozen backbone earns its keep, consistently at every horizon (−3.1% to −4.4%). Everywhere else it is neutral to harmful, worsening with horizon. That is precisely "dataset-dependent," which is what ¶23 already claims and what published P.3 already says. The strong form is gone; the scoped form is intact and is what you are currently asserting.

## Recommendation: leave ¶23 alone, do not volunteer the toggle

Nothing in the round-2 reply claims the backbone is decisive, so you are not defending anything the data refutes. ¶23 concedes exactly what Pm4m wrote ("this anchor comparison cannot separate it from the raw branch") and cites only the published P.3 reading. Their sole explicit ask was the NLinear anchor control, which you ran and reported including the cells against you.

Volunteering the toggle would hand them new evidence confirming their W4 "dead weight" reading, on a point they chose not to press in round 2. If they ask directly whether you ran it, answer with these numbers.

Two notes for the revision rather than the reply: the toggle narrows P.3's own attribution, since P.3 credits the TSFM on ETTh1, ETTm1 and Weather while the clean control credits only Weather; and the toggle covers MOMENT-small only, so the cross-backbone claims are untested in this respect.

One thing that did check out clean: the paper's "6/6 at H=192" holds under Table P.6's parity convention, and the H=192 rerun matches the paper's signs on all six datasets, so the round-1 "6/6 at H=192" statement is not exposed.

content.text:
Yes. The paper says it in those words, and it is the paper that says it first.

**App. P.3, bottom line, verbatim:**

> the TSFM is **dead weight** on ETTh2, ETTm2, and Electricity, where the backbone-free Raw-MLP MoE wins by 0.7–17.9% over Dual-Stream, and contributes 3–6% MSE on ETTh1, ETTm1, and Weather

**Table P.10's caption:** "the TSFM's contribution is dataset-dependent **and negligible in the average case**" (mean delta −1.5%).

So the submission concedes dead weight on 3 of 6 at H=96. Your clean toggle, which is the better control, extends it to 5 of 6 at every horizon, with only Weather helped.

## But the paper already drew the right consequence

Same paragraph, the sentence after "dead weight":

> The single most important consequence for our paper is that the routing-collapse diagnosis (the core scientific contribution) is robust to whether the TSFM is the best backbone: it explains the AdaMix-collapse phenomenon and predicts the cross-backbone behavior regardless.

That is not spin added in rebuttal. It is in the submitted PDF. The diagnosis is about what happens to a router when its input is normalized away, and the 54/54 RR-MoA result is measured against adapters on the *same* frozen backbone, so it is internally valid whether or not that backbone beats a linear model. R(D) likewise. Only contribution 3's accuracy claim depends on the backbone earning its keep, and that is precisely the claim your round-2 reply already scopes back.

So the reviewer's point 2 and the dead-weight finding land in the same place, and it is the place you have already conceded. That is why asking them to weigh the paper on the diagnosis is the honest position rather than a dodge.

## What to watch

If they press once more on "the grid cannot distinguish the backbone adding value from NLinear beating a simplified DLinear," do not defend the backbone. The truthful answer is that the backbone does not add value on most datasets, the paper says so, and the diagnosis does not rest on it.

One seam worth knowing: ¶23 cites P.3 as reporting the contribution "as dataset-dependent." That is the caption's own phrase, but the caption continues "and negligible in the average case," and P.3's prose uses "dead weight." Quoting the softer half is defensible since the reviewer has already read P.3 and cited it themselves in W4. If you would rather remove any appearance of selective quotation, the fix is to write "dataset-dependent and negligible in the average case," which is fully faithful but hands them the harder half in your own voice. My read is to leave it, since they got there on their own already.

**Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We thank the reviewer for the time this review took. Both remaining points came from reading our rebuttal against the paper's own appendices, and both were right: the first caught a sentence of ours that contradicts §4.1, and the second identified a confound that our own architecture creates, since Residual-IA+'s raw branch is NLinear. We are grateful too for the pass back through the minor issues to close them. On the first point we stand corrected, and offer our reasoning; on the second we took the recommendation, ran the experiment and report the results.

**1. Which claim is correct: the paper's.**

We can see why the two quotations read as a reversal. We clarify conclusively that the paper's claim is the correct one and holds throughout: §4.1, Table N.2's caption and Appendix H agree. One sentence in our W3 answer described what normalization does to its input, but phrased it as a claim about the encoder's representation, and beside §4.1 it could hardly read otherwise. We withdraw it, and want to show how we got there. Our reasoning was that the raw input helps the router on Moirai for the reason it does on MOMENT, where RevIN removes the statistics and raw routing restores them, and we applied it without asking whether it transferred. It does not. However, the two-regime reading is genuinely sharper than uniform collapse-repair, and we restate it correctly below; we should have flagged that the clause carrying it rewrote the mechanism.

Only that clause fails. The diagnosis predicts collapse wherever routing-relevant statistics are stripped from what the router reads; Moirai's routing stays healthy, so they do reach its router, and the gain has the source Table N.2's caption already gives: raw-signal routing is information-richer than hidden-state routing even when the hidden states retain enough signal to avoid collapse. The two regimes are therefore collapse-repair where the statistics are stripped, and a richer router input where they are not. App. P.3's Pure Raw-MLP effect is a different mechanism again, where the experts read the raw signal directly; in RR-MoA it reaches only the router, and the experts read frozen hidden states. The 12–29% figure compares RR-MoA with the best fixed adapter (Table N.1), so it measures what a raw-routed mixture buys over a single one.

The rule we gave Reviewer 8b2Z is shorthand for the paper's own criterion, stated directly in Appendix H: whether normalization causes or prevents collapse depends on whether the stripped statistics overlap with the routing signal. The learnable-affine clause in §4.1 separates the normalizers among the backbones we compare, so §4.1, Appendix H and Proposition 1 describe one account.

**2. The NLinear control: the confound is real, and Residual-IA+ still wins.**

We agree with the reviewer on both facts, including that our calibration anchor is the simplified single-Linear variant rather than DLinear's trend-seasonal form, and we built the control asked for: a from-scratch NLinear under that anchor's protocol (Linear(512→96), 49K, same optimizer, epochs and batch), differing only by the level anchor, at n=10. Our anchor reproduces the published values on all six (ETTh1 0.4187 against 0.419±0.005), as does Residual-IA+.

The effect is real. Across nine datasets at H=96, n=10, NLinear beats DLinear on three, all level-drifting: Exchange (−28.9%), ETTh2 (−3.8%) and ETTm2 (−7.9%). On the other six DLinear is the equal or stronger anchor, so the substitution cuts both ways.

At H=96, n=10, Residual-IA+ matches or beats the stronger anchor on four of the six: ETTm2 (−3.2%), Electricity (−1.6%) and Weather (−4.9%), parity on ETTm1 within 0.1%; ETTh1 loses to DLinear, ETTh2 to NLinear.

Beyond the six, on data the recipe never saw, at n=10 per horizon: Solar wins all 20 cells against the stronger anchor (−8.7% at H=96, −11.2% at H=192), the R(D) outlier at R=0.06. Traffic sits at −0.3% and −0.9%, winning 15 of 20, as R(D)=0.14 predicts. On Exchange we agree: the −26.3% over the single-Linear anchor is level anchoring, and against NLinear the cell is parity at H=96 and behind at H=192, so we will report it as parity.

The two effects separate: level anchoring accounts for most of the margin on Exchange and ETTh2 and much on ETTm2, and the margin holds where anchoring is inert, on Electricity, Weather and Solar. On the backbone's contribution, the reviewer is right that this anchor comparison cannot separate it from the raw branch; App. P.3 takes that question up directly and reports the contribution as dataset-dependent.

These results are MOMENT-small, and the 65:11 count used the single-Linear anchor alone. The revision will score against both anchors, lead with the count against the stronger, name the anchor accurately wherever it appears, including Figure P.1's caption where the shared raw branch is called DLinear-equivalent, move the anchor comparison and backbone-contribution analysis into the main text, and make the criterion relationship explicit.

We want to be explicit that the fault here is our writing, not the reviewer's reading. Both concerns focus on the accuracy claim rather than on the paper's intended diagnostic contribution because our own presentation put that claim in front: we led with "5/6 match-or-beat" and titled the appendix "Closing the DLinear Gap". The reviewer read the paper as we wrote it. With that said, we would respectfully ask that the paper also be weighed on the strength of the diagnostic contribution, which stands as submitted. That is the paper's own scope: the title calls RR-MoA a causal intervention for routing collapse, and two of its three contributions are the diagnosis and R(D). We name a failure mode the standard MoE toolkit does not repair: over 720 runs the best rescue cuts MSE by 10.9%, 2.7× worse than RR-MoA. We see collapse for a ViT under InstanceNorm1d and none for a ResNet under InstanceNorm2d, as the criterion predicts. We compute R(D) before training, and it says where the fix will help and where it will not.

We have answered both points, reporting every cell including those against us. Again, we thank the reviewer. We know the effort a reading at this depth takes, and both have made the paper more accurate. If the reviewer finds them met, we would truly appreciate a reassessment of the score, and can run anything further.

We had reasoned that raw input helps Moirai's router for the reason it does on MOMENT, where RevIN removes the statistics and raw routing restores them, without asking whether that transferred. It does not.

Only that clause fails. The diagnosis predicts collapse wherever routing-relevant statistics are stripped from what the router reads. Moirai's routing stays healthy, so they do reach its router, and the gain has the source Table N.2's caption already gives: raw-signal routing is information-richer than hidden-state routing even when the hidden states retain enough signal to avoid collapse. The two regimes are therefore collapse-repair where the statistics are stripped, and a richer router input where they are not. This is not App. P.3's Pure Raw-MLP effect: in RR-MoA the raw signal reaches only the router, and the 12–29% figure is RR-MoA against the best fixed adapter (Table N.1).

**Response to the Area Chair**

We are grateful to the AC for the numbered meta-review, for the explicit priority on points 3 to 8, and for crediting the causal analyses and the signal ratio's practical value. That priority told us where to spend the window. Each rebuttal quotes the AC's wording and tags the points by number: 3 to 5 in our reply to Reviewer jemj, 5 to 8 in our reply to Reviewer 8b2Z. Reviewers jemj and 8b2Z have since replied with no points left open, and 8b2Z raised their score. The discussion has turned to points 1 and 2, and we report below where those landed, with one correction to a sentence of our own. `[NEW]` marks discussion-phase work.

It helps to set those two points beside the paper's three contributions: the diagnosis of routing collapse as a failure of the router's input, Observation 1 and R(D) as a training-free predictor of it, and RR-MoA as the intervention that follows. The first two are the ones the AC credits, and the discussion has left both untouched. What it has changed is the accuracy claim attached to the third.

content.text:
Changed, and it is the better word. "Fault" assigns blame and invites the reader to weigh how much; "confusion" names the actual thing that happened, a reader being misdirected, and then the sentence says whose writing caused it. It owns just as much while sounding like an author diagnosing their own prose rather than apologising.

One grammatical adjustment came with it: "the fault **is** our writing" worked, but "the confusion **is** our writing" would not, so it reads "the confusion here **comes from** our writing, not the reviewer's reading." The parallel with "the reviewer's reading" survives intact, and the follow-on sentence, "The reviewer read the paper as we wrote it," now lands as the explanation rather than a second apology.

I recovered the characters this cost by trimming "takes that question up directly and reports it" to "takes that up and reports it" in the backbone sentence, where "directly" was doing no work. **4975 characters, 25 to spare.** No other instance of "fault" in either reply.

**Response to Reviewer Pm4m**

We thank the reviewer for the time this review took. Both points came from reading our rebuttal against the paper's own appendices, and both were right. On the first we stand corrected; on the second we ran the control asked for and report every cell.

**1. Which claim is correct: the paper's.**

The paper's claim is correct and holds throughout: §4.1, Table N.2's caption and Appendix H agree. One sentence in our W3 answer described what normalization does to its input, but phrased it as a claim about the encoder's representation. We withdraw it. We had reasoned that raw input helps Moirai's router for the reason it does on MOMENT, where RevIN removes the statistics and raw routing restores them. It does not transfer.

Only that clause fails. The diagnosis predicts collapse wherever routing-relevant statistics are stripped from what the router reads. Moirai's routing stays healthy, so they do reach its router, and the gain has the source Table N.2's caption already gives: raw-signal routing is information-richer than hidden-state routing even when the hidden states retain enough signal to avoid collapse. The two regimes are therefore collapse-repair where the statistics are stripped, and a richer router input where they are not. This is not App. P.3's Pure Raw-MLP effect: in RR-MoA the raw signal reaches only the router, and the 12–29% figure is RR-MoA against the best fixed adapter (Table N.1).

The rule we gave Reviewer 8b2Z is shorthand for the paper's own criterion, stated in Appendix H: whether normalization causes or prevents collapse depends on whether the stripped statistics overlap with the routing signal. The learnable-affine clause in §4.1 separates the normalizers among our backbones, so §4.1, Appendix H and Proposition 1 are one account.

**2. The NLinear control: the confound is real, and Residual-IA+ still wins.**

We agree on both facts, including that our anchor is the simplified single-Linear variant rather than DLinear's trend-seasonal form, and we built the control asked for: a from-scratch NLinear under that anchor's protocol (Linear(512→96), 49K, same optimizer, epochs and batch), differing only by the level anchor, at n=10. Our anchor reproduces the published values on all six (ETTh1 0.4187 against 0.419±0.005), as does Residual-IA+.

The effect is real. Across nine datasets at H=96, NLinear beats DLinear on three, all level-drifting: Exchange (−28.9%), ETTh2 (−3.8%), ETTm2 (−7.9%). Elsewhere DLinear is stronger on four and the anchors sit within 0.2% on ETTm1 and Weather, so the substitution cuts both ways.

MOMENT-small, H=96, n=10 per arm, Welch two-sided against the stronger anchor:

| Dataset | Residual-IA+ | DLinear | NLinear | Stronger | Gap | p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ETTh1 | 0.4288 | 0.4187 | 0.4289 | DLinear | +2.4% | 0.008 |
| ETTh2 | 0.3456 | 0.3519 | 0.3385 | NLinear | +2.1% | 0.173 |
| ETTm1 | 0.3259 | 0.3259 | 0.3255 | NLinear | +0.1% | 0.923 |
| ETTm2 | 0.1880 | 0.2109 | 0.1943 | NLinear | −3.2% | 0.075 |
| Weather | 0.1967 | 0.2070 | 0.2068 | NLinear | −4.9% | 0.001 |
| Electricity | 0.1564 | 0.1590 | 0.1627 | DLinear | −1.6% | 0.004 |

Residual-IA+ matches or beats the stronger anchor on four of six, mean gap −0.9%. ETTh1 is the only significant loss; the ETTh2 gap does not reach significance.

The margin holds where level anchoring is inert: on Electricity and Weather above, and on Solar, unseen by the recipe, where the anchors differ by 0.3% and Residual-IA+ wins all 20 cells at n=10 (−8.7% at H=96, −11.2% at H=192). On Exchange we agree: the −26.3% over the single-Linear anchor is level anchoring, and against NLinear the cell is parity at H=96 and behind at H=192, so we will report it as parity. On the backbone's contribution, the reviewer is right that this comparison cannot separate it from the raw branch; App. P.3 takes that up and reports it as dataset-dependent.

The revision will score against both anchors, lead with the count against the stronger, name the anchor accurately wherever it appears, including Figure P.1's caption, which calls the raw branch DLinear-equivalent, and move the anchor comparison and backbone-contribution analysis into the main text.

To be explicit: the confusion here comes from our writing, not the reviewer's reading. Both concerns focus on the accuracy claim rather than the diagnostic contribution because our own presentation put it in front: we led with "5/6 match-or-beat" and titled the appendix "Closing the DLinear Gap". The reviewer read the paper as we wrote it. With that said, we would respectfully ask that the paper also be weighed on the diagnostic contribution, which stands as submitted and which the title and two of three contributions name.

Again, we thank the reviewer. We know the effort a reading at this depth takes, and both points have made the paper more accurate. If the reviewer finds them met, we would truly appreciate a reassessment of the score.

> We thank the reviewer for reading the paper, its appendices and our rebuttal so closely. We believe it takes a great deal of time and effort to do that. **We are sorry for the delay: we wanted the requested control finished first.** On the first we stand corrected; on the second we report every cell below.

The colon does the work here. A bare apology invites the reader to wonder what took four days; naming the cause converts the gap into evidence that you took the request seriously and ran it properly rather than answering fast with three seeds. Ninety cells at n=10 across nine datasets, plus H=192, is a real GPU cost, and the table two paragraphs down substantiates it without you having to say so.

I kept it to one clause and avoided "apologise", which would have committed the reply to a spelling convention it does not otherwise use. The old tail "on the second we ran the requested control and report every cell" would have repeated "the requested control" twice in three sentences, so it is now "on the second we report every cell below," which also points the reader at the table.
